chapters.title: Chapter 1. Autumn in Molodoy Tud
chapters.html:
Autumn came into its own in Molodoy Tud reluctantly, like a late guest . For a long time, the sun continued to warm the meadows with a gentle hand, so that even as November approached, shy clover blossoms still raised their little candles, and tiny, delicate daisies went on blooming, pretending that nothing had changed. But that morning, the grass glimmered with a fragile veil of pale frost, and the night’s chill did not retreat until noon. The air already carried the unmistakable scent of wet fallen leaves and the breath of winter drawing near.

In the cosy little house by the river, where the air always smelled of dried herbs and water, birch logs were already crackling in the stove. Mr Otter pulled on his blue fisherman boots, dashed out onto the porch, filled a little bucket with clear, tinkling water from the swift-flowing Tudovka, and hurried back inside to put the kettle on and cook the morning porridge.

As he drew the water, he twitched his whiskers, sniffed the wind, shook his head, and gave a quiet whistle.

“Winter is on our doorstep. We have no time to lose.”

When the kettle on the stove began to hiss crossly, announcing that the water had come to a boil, Mr Otter went over to his son’s little bed and whispered:

“Time to get up, little Otterling. We have important things to do today.”

But the cozi downer was so wonderfully warm. Little Otterling buried his whiskered muzzle deep in the feather bed and gave a plaintive little whimper. Sleep had not yet let go of him, and he, Little Otterling, was quite unprepared to let go of sleep.

Mr Otter lowered himself onto the edge of the bed with a heavy but tender sigh and stroked his son’s warm back.

“Winter doesn’t ask whether you’re ready, little one. We need to see how the other animals are preparing for its arrival. And lend a hand if anyone needs help. Up you get, son. The porridge is on the table waiting for you”

After breakfast, they set off along the path that wound beside the Tudovka, heading upstream towards the bend in the river, where the sturdy Beaver Lodge could be seen. Even from a distance, they could hear the tapping and rustling. The Beavers had been already, eaten their breakfast, and got straight to work. Father Beaver was diligently patching the dam, while his younger son puffed and panted as he carried branches to him.

“Do you need a hand, neighbours?” Mr Otter asked politely.

Father Beaver wiped his paws on his apron, straightened up, and gave his handiwork a critical inspection.

“The river will freeze over in December, neighbour, and we must finish in time. Otherwise, the lodge could be swept away. This is no laughing matter. We’re managing on our own for now!”

A cheerful Mrs Beaver peeped out of the round window and offered their guests hot cranberry juice with honey. They each drank a mug, feeling the warmth spread through their paws, then set off again with renewed energy, following the banks where the alders had already shed more than half their leaves. The few that remained trembled on the branches in the wind, like forgotten handkerchiefs left out after washing.

On the mountainside, along the path to the deep woods, stood Fox’s house: a wooden cottage with intricately carved window frames. The mistress herself sat on the porch and grooming, her nose turned up to the wind, while tufts of fur went flying in every direction. Before winter, Fox was brushing out her old coat so that a new, thick winter one would grow in sooner.

*(The wind carries the russet fluff onto the beaver dam and presses it into the mud. Come spring, the softest, fluffiest grass will sprout there. The forest loses nothing.)*

“Oh, it’s you otters,” Fox sniffed, without turning around. “I see you’re out inspecting everyone, as though you’ve nothing better to do yourselves. Everything is perfectly fine here. My house is dry and warm. Simply marvellous.”

Mr Otter said nothing. He had noticed that the cottage door hung slightly crooked, and that the snow blizzard would inevitably whistle through the gap. But he knew there was little point in telling Fox how to look after her home. At last, he grumbled:

“Don’t go showing off, Fox. If you need help, just say so.”

“Well, I’m not sure,” she drawled haughtily. “I seem to recall you had a wonderful little comb. Mine has gone missing somewhere. And this old fur must be brushed out before the cold sets in. Otherwise, the new coat won’t grow properly.”

Fox turned away, as though she had done them an enormous favour.

“I’ll bring it,” Mr Otter said curtly.

“Just don’t be long. I have a great deal to do.”

“Is she asking for help?,” Little Otterling whispered when they had walked a little way off.

“She’s asking for a comb. That’s different,” Papa replied just as quietly. “But it’s still a kind of help. We simply pretend not to notice the difference.”

The fir trees on the slopes still stood green, but their colour had grown deeper and heavier, like cloth soaked through with icy water. Among the firs, on the stone terrace of an old manor house, a sleepy Bear sat in the rays of sunlight. He was sorting the pinecones the squirrels had brought to the storehouse and grumbling at the flighty little creatures for their carelessness.

Bear had come up with the idea of a squirrel storehouse long ago. Before that, the squirrels hid their supplies wherever they pleased, in the first pile of leaves they came across. Later, they would rush about in a panic, squeaking that they had forgotten where they had stashed their food. The fuss was so exhausting that it gave Bear a headache even in the deepest part of his winter sleep. So he had set aside one of the manor’s storerooms for their supplies.

Having given the squirrels his final instructions, Bear slowly turned towards Little Otterling and looked at him for a long, serious moment with his deep, ancient eyes.

“Little Otterling. I’m going to sleep. For a long time. All the way until spring.”

“But who will look after the forest?” Little Otterling asked in alarm.

“You will. And your dad. Keep an eye on things. And one more thing… make sure the cellar doesn’t flood. The spring waters will rise, and I’ll still be asleep. Check on it, will you?”

Bear held out a little amber stone: smooth and golden, a piece of pine resin in which a tiny pine needle had been trapped forever.

“This is for you to remember the sunny summer by, in case winter makes you sad. And one more thing… look after the forest. I’ve always done it myself. And now it’s your turn.”

Little Otterling nodded. The stone was warm and glowed like a captured sunbeam, dozing in the hollow of his paw.

Early evening came. It was not yet five pm, but twilight had already slipped down from the hills and tangled itself in the tops of the fir trees. Mr Otter and Little Otterling were on their way home.

A hot bathhouse awaited them there, while Mama Otter had spent the whole day bustling about the house. She had arranged jars of raspberry jam and pickles on the shelves in the cool pantry, hung dried mushrooms , and insulated the windows with duck down. She had even found time to visit Miss Fox and lend her the wonderful little comb made of willow twigs. When she returned, she lit the bathhouse stove and scent of burning birchwood drifted along the riverbank.

Along the length of the river, one by one, lanterns began to glow in the homes of the woodland and river creatures. Their little lights shimmered in the cold, dark water and winked at the stars in the high, deep blue sky.

Little Otterling clasped the warm amber stone more tightly in his paw. He gazed at the glowing lights and thought that as long as they kept shining, there was not anything to be afraid of.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Chaffinch
chapters.html:
The morning was cold and grey, with a proper winter chill in the air. The sun showed no hurry to warm the dark, swift-flowing Tudovka or the creatures who made their homes along its banks. The river moved sluggishly, almost reluctantly, and a damp, penetrating cold water, rose from the water.

Little Otter was the first to step outside. That was when he heard it.

*Ting-ting.*

A tiny sound, as though someone was gently tapping on a pane of glass from the other side.

A little chaffinch sat at the very edge of the landing. Its feathers were ruffled, eyes half-closed, little feet tucked beneath him. That little bird seemed to be asleep, but even in its sleep he trembled — whether from cold or fear, it was hard to tell.

“Dad!” Little Otterling called. “Come quickly! There’s a bird here, and it can’t fly.”

Mr. Otter came outside, took one look at the little bird, and crouched down beside it.

“A Chaffinch,” he said. “He has fallen behind its flock.”

“Why?”

“Because the flock moved on, and he couldn’t keep up. It happens sometimes. The wind may have blown him off course, or he just stopped for too long.” Dad paused. “Chaffinches arrive early in spring, when the air is still chilly, and stay late into autumn. This little fellow has stayed a little too long this year.”

Otterling dashed indoors and came back with his favourite red scarf. Mother had knitted it for him, and it was as light and warm as one of her hugs.

Little Otter drew the Chaffinch close to his chest and wrapped the scarf around him. The bird’s heart fluttered so fast that it seemed to be in a terrible hurry to get somewhere, even without the rest of its body.

A few minutes later, the Chaffinch had warmed up enough to speak. His voice was small and thin, but there was a stubborn note in it.

“I don’t know which way to go,” he said. “We were flying over the forest, and then the wind came, and I lost sight of everyone. I didn’t recognise anything around me. I flew round and round and finally landed. I thought I’d rest a little, then find them. But the flock was gone.”

“Where were you heading?” Little Otter asked.

“South,” said Chaffinch. “Everyone flies south. Only I don’t know where the south is.”

Mr Otter rose to his feet.

“Come along,” he said. “We’ll find someone else who’s heading south. There are plenty of kind-hearted creatures around here. Someone is surely going to help you find your way. But first, you need to warm up properly and have some breakfast. Come inside, little fellow. A mug of warm cranberry juice and a bowl of seeds will soon put you right.”

After breakfast, they set out to find some travelling companions.

The Sparrows lived beneath the roof of an old barn. They had a whole row of two-storey nests, complete with little terraces, and a signpost pointed the way, bearing the engraved name *Sparrovill*.

By day, the place was filled with an endless hubbub of chirping. Sunlight slipped through the gaps in the roof, laying golden stripes across the floor, where dust motes danced and whirled. The air smelled of dry grain, mice, and warmth — that particular kind of warmth found only beneath an old roof, where generations of little creatures have made their homes.

*(Sparrows are rather like household spirits, after all. They don't fly away or abandon their homes. Where they're born is where they spend the winter, too. People feed them, and in return, the sparrows keep the barns safe from mice and fill the yards with cheerful chirping, even on the greyest of days.)*

The Sparrow Governor sat on the ridge of the roof, a straw in his beak, surveying his domain.

“Welcome, Otters! A pleasure to receive you in Sparrovill. Do remember to leave a review and a few grains in the feeder by the entrance,” he chirped, with great importance.

“Hello, Governor,” said MrCOtter. “This little Chaffinch has fallen behind its flock and is looking for someone to fly south with.”

The Sparrow looked at the Chaffinch, then at the Otters, then back at the Chaffinch again.

“We don't migrate,” he explained. “We live here all year round. Winter can be hard, of course, but the people help us through it. We take good care of Sparrowville. There are warm little nooks beneath the barn roof, and our feeders are kept full.”

“You really never fly away?” Little Otterling asked.

“Never,” said the Sparrow. “We're like household spirits. Where would we go? This is our Home.”

He took a closer look at the Chaffinch.

“Why not stay with us?” he suggested. “We're a friendly lot. We'll find you a nest of your own. You can spend the winter here, and in spring you can decide what you'd like to do. Who knows? You might even choose to stay.”

Chaffinch thought it over. Then he shook his head.

“I wouldn't know how to spend the winter here,” he said. “And besides, there's my flock. They'll be waiting for me out there. In the south.”

“Well,” said Sparrow, shaking his head, “then you should try the Ducks. They'll certainly be flying south. They gather for the journey every year. Only they do take their time about it.”

The ponds in the manor park were old, overgrown, and dark. The water lay almost motionless, reflecting the trees, the sky, and the low grey clouds. Willows trailed their branches in the water along the banks, while the reeds rustled in the wind with a dry, mournful whisper.

In autumn, the ponds froze before anything else. A thin, smooth, dark skin of ice formed across the surface, almost impossible to see. You could tell it was there only by its faint sheen, or by the way the water suddenly stopped trembling.

Right at the water's edge stood a little duck house, built of planks, low and squat, with a moss-covered roof. The boards were of different widths and colours — grey, brown, some faded almost to white — so that the whole house looked as though it had been stitched together from scraps of fabric. It gave the place a charming, patchwork look, with colours that shimmered like the feathers of a drake.

A black noticeboard hung on the outer wall. Two pieces of paper were pinned to it. One bore a picture of Fox with a red exclamation mark beside it. On the other, someone had written with black pencil:

DEPARTURE — WAITING FOR ICE

The Ducks strutted busily around their colourful little house, preened their feathers, and argued among themselves. Their reflections trembled in the dark pond water, as though a second, equally restless nation of ducks lived beneath the surface.

By the river, Captain Duck sat comfortably in a rocking chair, gazing dreamily at the clouds. He seemed to be whistling a tune called *Only the Stars Fly Higher Than Ducks*. Or perhaps it was *Don't Cry, my Baby, Your Duck will return*. It was difficult to recognise the melody through his whistling.

“Hello, Captain,” said Mr Otter. “When are you flying south?”

“When the ice comes,” the Captain replied.

He sprang up so abruptly at the unexpected greeting that he nearly toppled into the pond, but saved himself just in time with a dashing flap of his wings.

“We need open water,” he explained. “As long as the water stays open, we can feed. The moment ice begins to form along the banks, we're off. We can't wait until the whole pond freezes over. By then, we won't be able to take off.”

“And when will the ice come?” asked the Chaffinch.

“Perhaps in a week,” said the Captain. “Perhaps in two. We wait and see. If you want to fly with us, you can stay here. We're always glad to have company.”

Then he resumed his whistling, this time with a tune about how *A Hero's Journey Never Frightens the Brave*.

The chaffinch looked down at its little feet. They were trembling.

“I can't hold out that long,” it whispered.

Little Otterling wrapped the scarf more tightly around the bird.

“he’s freezing,” he said. “He needs help now.”

The Duck Captain shook his head.

“There's nothing I can do,” he said. “We're waiting .”

They stood beside the pond. The Chaffinch fell silent. Little Otter looked at it, not knowing what to say. The sparrows stayed where they were, the ducks were still waiting, and the Chaffinch couldn't do either.

Then Mr Otter spoke.

“There are still the Rooks.”

Little Otter looked up.

“The Rooks will be leaving any day now,” Dad said. “In great flocks. They're heading south. Perhaps they'll take you along.”

In the manor park stood a row of old linden trees, tall, black, and bare, their branches interwoven as though someone had deliberately woven them together. Among those branches hung the rooks' nests, large, dark, curious knots of twigs — dozens upon dozens of them.

This was Rook County.

The Chief Rook called himself the Count and claimed that his family descended, through thirty-three generations, from the very first bird on earth. He had even taken the trouble to peck the entire family tree into the trunk of the oldest and largest linden tree.

Now anyone who wished could study all thirty-three generations of the Count's illustrious ancestors. The tree listed not only their names, but also their hobbies and character traits. One thing was perfectly clear from the carving: every rook loved to fly, and every rook was a proud, independent bird.

*(Old rook nests are like little fortresses, after all. Owls shelter in them through the winter, squirrels hide from the rain in them, and when the spring comes, the rooks return as though they had never left. )*

“A chaffinch?” said the Count, looking the little bird over. “A bit on the small side.”

“He can fly,” Little Otter insisted. “He just fell behind.”

“Can you fly?” the Rook asked.

“I can,” said the Chaffinch.

“And you won't fall behind?”

“I'll do my best.”

The Count studied it for a long time. At last, he nodded.

“We don't fly fast,” he said. “But we don't wait, either. So don't be late. We leave at dawn tomorrow. You'll find it easier in the flock. The wind won't buffet you so much there. You can fly in the middle.”

The Chaffinch looked at Little Otter. Little Otter nodded.

“Go,” he said. “I'll be waiting for you.”

The morning was cold and clear. A flock rose above the park — dozens upon dozens of little black specks, with one tiny speck among them, smaller than all the rest. The Chaffinch flew in the middle of the flock, sheltered from the buffeting wind.

Little Otter stood on the landing, waving his paw. Papa Otter stood beside him.

“Will he come back?” Little Otter asked.

“He will,” Dad assured him. “Chaffinches are among the first birds to return in early spring, before the ice has even melted from the river. He'll come back and tell us what he saw and whom he met. There'll be all sorts of stories — about the sea, the mountains, other rivers and forests.”

Little Otterling gazed at the sky for a long time. At last, he turned and went home.

He followed the riverbank, watching the water curl into little whirlpools. Yellow leaves spun round and round in them, as though someone was stirring autumn with a spoon.

He watched it and thought about his new friend, who would return to him in spring from faraway lands. And how wonderful it is, that they had found travelling companions for him in time.

chapters.title: Chapter 3. The Little Red Trousers
chapters.html:
At the edge of the old manor park stood a linden tree. It was a very old tree, with a thick trunk and a hollow inside. And in that hollow was a school.A school for squirrels.

A little wooden sign hung above the entrance. It read:

**SQUIRREL SCHOOL**

The walls inside were smooth and warm, sealed with fragrant resin. The blackboards were made of pieces of dark bark. There were even a few rules pinned up beside the entrance:

**Do not gnaw the blackboards.**

**No quarrelling on the branches.**

**And no nutshells on the floor!**

There were no ordinary desks or chairs. The pupils sat on branches arranged at different heights, depending on how tall they were and how well they could climb.

Their teacher was called Tuck. He was an elderly squirrel with silver tufts on his ears. He was strict, but fair, and he knew everything there was to know about the forest.

In one corner stood a large basket filled with cones — the school's winter store. And when the weather grew especially cold, a little stove kept the hollow warm.

The school even had a playground: a sturdy branch stretching out from the trunk, where the pupils could run about during breaks.

It was a happy school, and the squirrels loved it.

But there was one thing that happened every autumn which made life rather complicated for its pupils.They changed their coats.

In summer, squirrels wore russet fur, the colour of fallen leaves and warm sunshine. But as autumn drew to a close, their coats gradually turned grey, helping them blend in with the bare branches and the winter woods.

By November, almost everyone had changed.

Almost everyone — except Annie.

Annie's body had already turned grey, but her little trousers were still bright russet-red. They looked as though a piece of summer had somehow stayed behind.

At first, nobody paid much attention. But then Tinnie and Winnie, two squirrels who sat together on the branch behind Annie, began to whisper and giggle.

“Look at Annie Red-Trousers!”

“Perhaps she forgot to change!”

They tried to hide their laughter behind their paws, but Annie could hear every word.

It hurt most when they laughed at her together.

After that, Annie began to dread break time. She would slip away from the others and sit by herself on a branch, pretending to be busy looking for something in the bark.

One afternoon, she went with her mother to the marsh to pick cranberries. The ground was damp, and the paths were covered with fallen leaves. As they walked, Annie noticed a patch of smooth grey clay near the water.

She stopped and looked at it.

It was almost exactly the same colour as her new winter coat.

An idea came into her head.

If she covered her red trousers with clay, perhaps nobody would notice them. Perhaps Tinnie and Winnie would stop laughing.

That evening, when the house was quiet and everyone had gone to bed, Annie crept outside. She found the patch of grey clay and carefully rubbed it over her little trousers until the bright russet colour disappeared.

She went to sleep feeling rather pleased with herself.

The next morning, she walked into school with her head held high.

Nobody laughed. Annie felt a little flutter of relief. But then, during break time, someone made a snowball and threw it at her. It landed right on her trousers.

The snow melted almost at once, and the wet clay began to slide off. A moment later, Annie's bright red trousers appeared again — only now they were streaked with muddy brown patches.

“Oh, look!” cried Tinnie. “Annie Dirty-Trousers!”

Winnie burst out laughing.

Annie could not bear it any longer. She turned and ran home as fast as her little paws could carry her.

She rushed inside, climbed onto her bed and began to cry.

“I'm never going back to school!” she sobbed. “Never!”

Her mother came in at once and sat beside her.

“What has happened, darling?”

Annie tried to explain, but the words kept getting caught in her tears.

“They laughed at me again. I want to be grey. I want to look like everyone else.”

Mama drew her a little closer and gently brushed a strand of fur away from her face.

“I know, darling.”

She picked up a damp cloth and began carefully wiping the last traces of clay from Annie's fur. Then she took Annie's little paws in hers and held them for a moment.

“Does it still hurt?” she asked.

Annie nodded.

Mama said nothing. She simply stayed beside her, stroking her back until Annie's sobs grew quieter.

After a while, she fetched the little silver mirror and held it up so Annie could see herself.

“Look,” she said softly. “There you are.”

Annie looked at her reflection. Her fur was grey, her cheeks were pink from crying, and her trousers were still bright red.

“But they laughed at me,” she whispered.

“I know.” Mama smiled gently. “Sometimes, when others laugh, we start wishing we were someone else. Someone who wouldn't be noticed.”

She gave Annie's paw a little squeeze.

“But you don't have to change your colours to make other people happy. And you don't have to laugh along when something hurts.”

Annie looked down at her paws.

“What should I do tomorrow?”

Mama thought for a moment.

“Go to school. Stand tall, look them in the eye, and tell them how you feel. You don't need to shout. You don't need to hide. Just let them see you as you are.”

“And if they laugh again?”

“Then we'll think about what to do next. You won't have to face it alone.”

Mama kissed the top of Annie's head.

“Now, let's get those trousers clean. I think they've had quite enough of the marsh for one day.”

For the first time that evening, Annie gave a little smile.

The next morning, Annie went to school.

She was still a little nervous, but she remembered what Mama had said. She walked into the hollow, found her branch and sat down.

Tinnie and Winnie were already there. They glanced at her trousers and began whispering again.

But this time, Annie did not look away.

Just then, Mika, a squirrel from the next branch, came over.

“Annie, I think your trousers are lovely,” he said. “You're the prettiest little squirrel in the whole school.”

Annie blushed.

Tinnie and Winnie exchanged a glance. They seemed rather surprised that someone could actually like Annie's red trousers.

When the lesson ended, Annie stood up.

“My name is Annie,” she said clearly. “And I have red trousers. They'll turn grey when the time comes. But for now, this is how they are. And I'm not going to cover them in clay just to make things easier for you. They're my trousers, and I like them.”

She paused and looked at Tinnie and Winnie.

“And I know you were laughing at me. I saw you hiding behind your paws.”

Tinnie and Winnie looked down at their feet.

“We're sorry, Annie,” Tinnie said quietly.

“Yes,” Winnie added. “We shouldn't have laughed.”

Annie looked at them for a moment. She was still hurt, but she was glad they had apologised.

“Thank you,” she said.

And then, as though nothing particularly extraordinary had happened, the squirrels went outside to play.

They made snowballs and built a little snow fort. This time, everyone took care not to throw snowballs at anyone's trousers.

The days went by, and December arrived.

Annie's red trousers slowly began to fade. First they turned a pale russet, then a soft greyish brown. By January, they were almost the same colour as the rest of her winter coat.

But Annie no longer minded.

She had learnt that there was nothing wrong with being a little different. And she had discovered something important: she did not need to hide who she was just because someone else did not understand her.

Besides, she knew that when spring came, her trousers would turn russet again.

And this time, she was rather looking forward to it.

chapters.title: Chapter 4. Thin Ice
chapters.html:
By the beginning of December, the snow had settled in earnest and showed no sign of melting. It lay smooth and white and soft upon the ground. By lunchtime there was quite enough of it for snowball fights, snow forts and even the making of a proper snowman.

The young squirrels poured out of school and onto the broad branch, cheering with delight.

“Snow! Real snow!”

Tinnie and Winnie at once began making snowballs and throwing them at one another. Mika scampered to the edge of the branch and peered down into the park.

“Let's make a great big snow bear!” he cried. “It'll freeze solid in the frost and look just like a real one!”

“Just like a real one!” cried Tinnie and Winnie.

“Just like a real one!” laughed Annie.

And off they all went, tumbling down into the park.

The old linden trees stood beneath the snow as though they had dressed themselves in heavy white coats. Their branches drooped under the weight, and every now and then a soft, heavy clump of snow slipped from a bough and fell with a muffled thump.

The ponds had frozen over, their dark, smooth surfaces covered by an even layer of snow, like a great quilt of freshly beaten down.

(Pond ice is a crafty thing. It freezes before river ice because the water in a pond stands still, while a river is always moving. But pond ice is thin and deceptive, and the creatures of the wood know this very well. It is only the little ones who sometimes forget.)

The young squirrels began rolling snowballs. First little ones, then bigger ones, and then enormous ones — so enormous that two of them could hardly move them together. They rolled them all over the park, laughing, tumbling into the snow, scrambling up again, brushing themselves off and setting to work once more. The snow squeaked beneath their paws. Snowflakes settled on their fur and melted there, leaving it damp and shining.

“Another one!” Mika called. “One more! And this one goes right on top!”

He rolled and rolled, paying no attention to where he was going. Beneath the snow, it was impossible to tell where the bank ended and the pond began. He kept pushing the great ball onwards, until suddenly there came a small, sharp crack beneath his paws, like a dry twig snapping.

The ice gave way.

And Mika plunged headfirst into the water.

The water was icy, sharp as a thousand little needles. It seized his breath, closed round him and dragged him down. Mika thrashed about, cried out, swallowed a mouthful of water and cried out again.

The young squirrels rushed to the edge. Tinnie and Winnie screamed. Annie stood frozen with fright.

“A branch!” someone shouted. “Quick, get a branch!”

A branch was thrust towards Mika. He caught hold of it, but his paws kept slipping, and it was far too short. He sank beneath the water once more, then surfaced again, his eyes wide and round with terror.

“Hold on!” Annie cried. “Hold on!”

But she could see that he would not be able to hold on for long. The branch was thin, the ice around him was fragile, and it would take only one more moment for someone else to fall in after him.

And then Annie turned and ran.

She ran through the park, across the yard and towards the school. But the school was empty. Teacher Tuck had already gone off on his own grown-up squirrel business.

There was no point in running home, either. Mama had gone to the village with the other squirrels. The sparrows had asked them to help sort the grain in their barn, and had promised to share some of their stores in return for the help.

Annie stopped for a moment, panting hard, and suddenly understood: there was nobody. Nobody nearby who could help.

And then she remembered the river.

She set off towards the Tudovka.

The snow was deep, and her paws sank into it. She stumbled and fell, picked herself up and ran on. The forest stood all around her, white and silent. Twilight had begun to gather — not dark yet, but soft and blue, the sort of twilight in which the world seems a little unreal, like an old watercolour painting. The shadows of the trees stretched across the snow, and the cold was creeping into her paws.

*I shan't make it,* Annie thought. *I shan't make it in time.*

She ran on, hearing her heart pounding, the snow crunching beneath her paws, and, somewhere far away in the park, the cries of the young squirrels.

And then, quite suddenly, she heard laughter.

The slope beside the Tudovka was long and gentle, and the snow lay upon it smooth and untouched. Some young creatures were sledging down it on an old wooden sledge with curled-up runners. Otterling was sitting at the front, Beaverling behind him, and together they came rushing down towards the very edge of the water, where the sledge always came to a halt against a bank of snow.

“Again!” Otterling shouted.

“Again!” Beaverling shouted back.

They scrambled up the slope, dragging the sledge by its rope, and whizzed down once more. Snow flew into their faces; they shook it off and climbed up again. The slope glittered in the winter light, and two deep, shining tracks marked the path of the runners.

Annie burst out of the forest.

“Otterling! Beaverling!” she cried. “Mika's fallen through the ice! He's drowning in the pond!”

Otterling dropped the rope. Beaverling let go of the sledge. They looked at one another for just a moment — and then they were off.

At the pond, everything was quiet and frightening.

Tinnie and Winnie stood at the edge, crying loudly. Mika was clinging to the broken rim of the ice, but his paws were growing weak. Every now and then his head disappeared beneath the water, only to appear again a moment later.

Beaverling reached him first. He did not stop to think. He simply lay down on the ice near the edge, spreading his paws wide for balance, and stretched out his tail towards Mika.

A beaver's tail is broad, flat, scaly and strong — rather like a little rescue board. Mika caught hold of it with both paws.

“Pull!” Beaverling shouted.

Otterling seized Beaverling by the hind legs. Annie and Tinnie grabbed hold of Otterling. Winnie caught Annie. And all together, digging their paws into the snow, they pulled with all their might.

Mika came flying out of the water like a cork and landed on the snow.

He was trembling violently, his teeth chattering. His fur was soaked and clung to his little body, and he could not utter a word.

Otterling took off his warm hooded jacket and wrapped it around Mika. Then he sat down beside him, put his arms around him and held him close.

“It's okay,” he said. “ You're safe now”

Mika gave a little sob and closed his eyes.

The young squirrels stood around them, silent and wide-eyed. After a while, Tinnie spoke, very quietly, almost in a whisper.

“We saw where he was rolling the snowball. We saw. And nobody said anything.”

“I thought he was only playing,” Winnie whispered. “He always does that — just keeps rolling and rolling without looking.”

“But we should have told him,” Annie said softly. “We should have shouted, ‘Mika, stop! The pond is there!’ But I didn't. None of us did.”

She looked at the pond — dark and frightening, with a black patch of open water near the bank. Then she looked at the white snow lying so smoothly and softly over the ice, so peacefully, as though nothing at all had happened.

“The ice is deceptive,” Annie said. “It looks solid, but there's water underneath. And it's not only ponds. Rivers and lakes too. Wherever there's water, the ice is thin at first. It has to grow stronger before it's safe.”

Otterling lifted his head. He was still holding Mika close, and the little squirrel was beginning to stop trembling.

“Dad told me,” Otterling said, “that the first ice is like the first snow. Beautiful, but fragile. You must never go out on it. Not on a pond, not on a river, not on a lake. Not until the grown-ups say it's safe. Until then, we must stay on the bank and look.”

Mika lifted his head. His eyes were red, but he was beginning to smile — a small, rather guilty smile.

“I won't do it again,” he whispered. “I thought I knew where the bank was. But the snow had covered everything.”

“Nobody can tell,” Otterling said. “You can't see a thing beneath the snow. That's why you must stick to familiar paths, and never go off on your own.”

He got to his feet, helped Mika up and took him by the paw.

“Come along,” he said. “Let's get him home.”

Mika nodded. He walked leaning against Otterling, still shivering a little, but carefully looking about him.

And all the while, the snow continued to fall.

Soft, white and silent, it settled on the pond, the river, the roofs of little houses and the branches of the trees. It hid everything beneath it: thin ice, deep holes and sharp stones. The snow made the world look smooth and beautiful. But now the young creatures knew that such beauty called for care.

By the time they reached Tudovka, evening had come. The lanterns were glowing, and warm golden light shone from the windows of the little houses by the river.

In every home to which the young creatures returned, a hot supper was waiting — and, most of all, the warm embrace of their parents.
